timeline.subtitle: The under-a-minute fix, based on NCSC and NIST guidance
timeline.narration: Most accounts aren't hacked. They're guessed from a list. Here's the fix, in under a minute.

timeline.heading: Most common passwords in breached accounts (NCSC, 2019)
timeline.narration: The UK's National Cyber Security Centre found one, two, three, four, five, six on twenty-three million breached accounts.

timeline.heading: Length beats complexity (if the password is chosen at random)
timeline.y_label: Strength in bits (each bit doubles the guesses)
timeline.narration: Length beats complexity. Four random words match eight random symbols, and are far easier to remember. Six words beat both, as long as a generator picks them.

timeline.heading: What NIST's 2025 password rules say
items: At least 15 characters when it's the only login factor
No forced mix of capitals, digits and symbols
No scheduled resets, only after a known breach
Every new password checked against breach lists
timeline.narration: NIST's 2025 rules agree: fifteen characters minimum, no forced symbols, no scheduled resets, and checks against breach lists.

timeline.heading: Do this today
items: Install a password manager and let it generate passwords
Make its master password four or more random words
Turn on two-factor or a passkey, starting with your email
timeline.narration: So, today: get a password manager, use four random words as its master password, turn on two-factor for your email first, and check have I been pwned dot com.
